question: Europe has many defibrillators installed in all kinds of public spaces – both indoors and outdoors – for use in an emergency by anyone with basic first-aid knowledge to save the lives of people suffering a heart attack. These defibrillators have a limited lifetime after which their correct functioning is no longer guaranteed, particularly as from 10 years after their installation.

As such, they need maintenance, especially when installed outside, where they are exposed to moisture and dust, and their batteries are affected by climatic conditions, more so than when installed indoors. The expiry date of the batteries and electrodes and the dates of the regular maintenance checks, etc. must thus be displayed on every defibrillator. 1.
Can the Commission state whether there is any monitoring of the number of defibrillator devices installed across Europe and of their state of maintenance?

Are there any programmes for replacing old defibrillators with new generation defibrillators, which can also provide the additional information needed to provide first aid pending the arrival of health professionals?
What strategy does the Commission have to better inform the public on how these emergency devices can be used by all members of the public and to organise first aid courses for them?
answer: According to Article 168(7) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, Member States are responsible for the definition of their health policy and for the organisation and delivery of health services and medical care. The responsibilities of the Member States shall include the management of health services and medical care and the allocation of the resources assigned to them.

The questions raised by the Honourable Member concern the management of health services and medical care, which are in the remit of the individual Member States. The Commission, however, supports the Member States in the area of public health.

In particular, the ‘Healthier Together’ — EU non-communicable diseases (NCDs) initiativ e (1) supports the Member States in their efforts to reduce the burden of major NCDs, such as cardiovascular diseases. The initiative supports knowledge sharing, the exchange of best practices between the Member States, and activities to improve health literacy and awareness among the population.

The EU provides financial support under the EU4Health programme (2) to complement the policies of the Member States by pursuing to improve and foster health, protect people, enhance access to medicinal products and medical devices and strengthen health systems.

The Member States may decide to organise specific awareness campaigns at national level with the aim of increasing knowledge on the use of defibrillators for resuscitation in the case of cardiac arrest.
